title: Sequence-length fragmentation probe - runtime field notes
content:
Quick summary:
- Goal: understand how a mixed client mix (short/medium/long contexts) impacts throughput and tail latency when the runtime switches attention/kv-cache kernels and when sequence-fragmentation heuristics kick in.
- Found a reproducible throughput cliff when long sequences make up >18% of concurrent inflight requests while short requests remain frequent — appears tied to repeated kernel selection changes and partial KV cache eviction/rehydration cost rather than pure GPU memory pressure.

Experiment plan (running in staging GPU pool G-8xA):
- Model: llama2-13b-int8 (quantized variant used for stable runs).
- Ingress mix: 50% short (avg len 32 tokens), 30% mid (avg 256), 20% long (avg 2048) — synthetic client generator to emulate product mix.
- Arrival process: Poisson base with scheduled microbursts (5s at +200% qps every 30s) to stim switching.
- Cache state: runs toggled between: cold (kill worker then spin up), partially warm (clients issue short-prefill then long), fully warm (long prefix preloaded).
- Runtime flags: --batching=continuous, --max-batch-tokens=4096, --enable-fragmentation-heuristic=true, --kvcache-eviction=soft, --kernel-switch-threshold=1024
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec (aggregated), model GPU util, kernel-switch-count (custom metric), kvcache-miss-rate.

Representative command used to drive bench (simplified):
python bench_driver.py --qps 600 --mix 50,30,20 --seqs 32,256,2048 --burst-schedule 30,5,2x --duration 20m --target-host staging-infer-01:443 --warm-prefix false

Raw highlights from a 20m run (nov 06):
- Avg qps offered: 612
- Achieved tokens/sec: 78k (stable until minute ~7)
- Kernel-switch-count (per-gpu per-min): 38 -> spiked to 124 at minute 7
- KV cache miss-rate: 2.1% baseline -> jumped to 8.7% during cliff
- Latency windows (aggregated):
  - p50: 38ms -> 45ms (post-cliff)
  - p95: 110ms -> 290ms
  - p99: 320ms -> 1.1s (worst of run)

ASCII timeline (tokens/sec aggregated, sampled per 30s):
[00:00] 78k | [01:00] 77k | [02:00] 75k | [03:00] 76k | [04:00] 74k | [05:00] 73k | [06:00] 60k <-- start cliff
[07:00] 46k | [08:00] 42k | [09:00] 55k | [10:00] 67k --> recovery

Observations / hypotheses:
1) Kernel switching is expensive: when the runtime switches attention/FFT kernels (short-path vs long-path) repeatedly, we see a latency tail amplification. The metric kernel-switch-count correlates tightly with p99.
2) Fragmentation heuristic (splitting long requests into smaller fragments to fit batching) reduces peak memory but seems to interact poorly with KV cache warming. Frequent fragmentation creates many small kv cache entries that are short-lived and cause thrashing.
3) Partial warm state is the worst-case: fully cold has predictable high latency but recovers; fully warm remains stable. The intermittent long requests that interleave with short ones are the trigger.
4) Microbursts amplify the problem because they temporarily increase inflight short requests that cause kernel selection to favor short-kernel fast-path, then long requests re-enter and cause expensive kernel migration.

Micro-trace snippet (from trace id trace:2025-11-06T07:12:23):
- request-4829 (short): route -> batch-140 -> short-kernel -> p50
- request-4830 (short): route -> batch-141 -> short-kernel
- request-4831 (long): route -> batch-142 -> fragmentation-> fragment-0 -> long-kernel initialization (kv-lookup) -> long-kernel -> fragment-1 -> miss -> kv-evict->rehydrate -> p99 spike

Experiment variations tried:
- Increasing --kernel-switch-threshold to 2048: reduced switch-count by ~40%, p99 improved but p50 regressed slightly (tradeoff).
- Turning off fragmentation heuristic: tokens/sec dropped 12% due to inability to pack long requests, but tail improved modestly (p99 -18%).
- Aggressive kvcache retention (no soft-evict for 90s): reduced miss-rate to 1.3% and tail stabilized, but GPU mem footprint rose ~6% and fewer concurrent long requests were fit.
- Request prioritization (soft-priority lanes for long requests): smoothed tail but increased short-request p50 by ~8ms.

Quick actionable takeaways:
- Short term (safe): increase kernel-switch-threshold from 1024 -> 1536 for staging pools where mixed sequence-profile expected. Add a soft cooldown window after switching where fragmentation is suppressed for N seconds to let KV cache stabilize.
- Medium term: implement a lightweight kernel-selection predictor (cache recent seq-length distribution per worker) so we avoid unnecessary kernel reinit when a single long request is predicted to be transient.
- Long term: revisit fragmentation strategy — instead of fragmenting into many small kv entries, reuse a dedicated long-request slab that shares cache entries for fragments of the same parent request.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Is the cost mainly host->device kernel reinitialization (context) or is it lower-level cuBLAS/cuda kernel selection overhead? Need more low-level profiling (NSys) during a controlled kernel-switch event.
- How does this interact with quantized kernel variants (we used int8; fp16 might behave differently on kernel-switch cost).
- What are customer-visible thresholds? Our heuristics should be parameterized per customer tier (dedicated vs hosted).

Next steps / TODOs:
- [ ] Run NSys capture during induced kernel-switch spike (target: staging-infer-03) — assigned to Arjun. Due: 2025-11-12.
- [ ] Prototype per-worker recent-seq-distribution predictor (POC 2d) — assigned to me. Due: 2025-11-14.
- [ ] Add metric kvcache-live-entries-per-request to help identify fragmentation churn — quick instrumentation MR by Mira.
- [ ] Run same mix against fp16 variant to compare kernel-switch costs (safety check).

Notes to self: keep this doc lightweight — it's a scratchpad for the team's immediate triage. When we have NSys traces and kernel-level evidence, move a distilled runbook into confluence and attach sample traces + commands.

Random aside (observational): during the worst tails, GPU util drops ~12% (likely due to CPU-side stalls while rehydrating KV entries) — worth instrumenting host-side thread stalls (spin/wait) in the runtime.

End of notes.
